verses.translation_literal: God of vengeances, YHWH! God of vengeances, shine forth!
verses.translation_dramatic: God of vengeances, LORD! God of vengeances, blaze out into the light!
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with a cry, not a greeting, and the cry is doubled so that it echoes in a stone courtyard. Actors should place the first 'God of vengeances' as a gasp and the second as a demand. The plural 'vengeances' is in the Hebrew; the KJV's 'to whom vengeance belongeth' turns a title into a sentence and flattens it into a single abstract noun. Here God is addressed as the one whose very name is acts of redress, the way an ancient Near Eastern king is the source of verdicts. This is not blood-lust: in a world with no police, a victim without a patron relied on the god to be the court of last appeal, and 'vengeance' (נְקָמָה) is the enforcement of justice, closer to 'a judicial reckoning'.

The KJV also renders the last word 'shew thyself', which loses the picture. הוֹפִיעַ is the verb of light, of the sun breaking over a ridge, and Metzudat Zion ties it to 'He shone forth from Mount Paran' (Deut 33:2). The people are asking God to come out of hiding and appear as the sunrise does, visible to all.

philological_notes.note: A plural of intensity: not one act of vengeance but the whole domain of redress. KJV's 'vengeance belongeth' turns the title into a clause. The sense is judicial reckoning, not private spite.
A verb of light: to shine out, appear radiantly. Used of God's appearing at Sinai/Paran in Deut 33:2.

verses.translation_literal: Lift yourself up, judge of the earth! Return a recompense upon the proud.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, judge of all the earth. Stand up on your bench, and let what the proud have earned fall back on their own heads.
verses.directors_commentary: Two imperatives, one posture and one act. 'Lift yourself up' (הִנָּשֵׂא) is the move of a judge getting to his feet to pronounce sentence, or a king rising from the throne. The KJV's 'Lift up thyself' is close to the Hebrew but archaic; the reflexive Niphal means 'carry yourself high', 'be exalted', and the target is deliberate: the proud (גֵּאִים) are the ones who have exalted themselves, so the psalm asks God to out-lift them. Ibn Ezra notes this is set against the proud. The word 'recompense' (גְּמוּל) is something done to a person in return for what they did; in the KJV's 'reward' it reads like a prize. Here it is a payment in kind, and the verb 'return' (הָשֵׁב, literally 'make come back') makes it a boomerang.

philological_notes.note: Niphal imperative, 'lift yourself up', 'be exalted'. Said to a judge, it is the call to rise and act. Radak links it with God's own word through the prophets, 'now I will be exalted' (Isa 33:10).
What is dealt out in return for a deed, for good or ill. Here the bad kind: the proud get back what they gave.

verses.translation_literal: Until when, wicked ones, YHWH, until when will wicked ones exult?
verses.translation_dramatic: How long, LORD? How long will the wicked, the wicked, go on exulting?
verses.directors_commentary: The cry of 'how long?' is the standard lament, and here it is split by the divine name and then doubled, the way a person says it when the first time was not heard. The Hebrew has 'wicked ones' (רְשָׁעִים) set before the verb in each half, so the word itself hangs, an unfinished accusation, until 'exult' lands: Hebrew gives the subject first, English must be coaxed to do the same. The KJV's 'triumph' is a fair guess but leans military; יַעֲלֹזוּ means to exult, to jump for joy, to be in high spirits, and Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'rejoice'. What stings is the sound: the wicked are celebrating, loudly, in public. Radak says the time has been very long for us and they speak 'weighty words' against God. Play the second 'how long' lower and harder than the first.

philological_notes.note: The formula 'until when', repeated here for emphasis. It is the stock opening of the lament psalm, and here it is aimed at the delay of justice rather than at suffering.
To exult, rejoice with abandon; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'they rejoice'. KJV 'triumph' overshoots toward a victory.

verses.translation_literal: They gush forth, they speak arrogance; they praise themselves, all workers of wickedness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their mouths are springs, and what pours from them is insolence. They talk and talk, and praise themselves, every last one of the men who work evil.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood shifts from lament to accusation, and the verbs come like a tap left open. יַבִּיעוּ is used of water welling from a spring (and of 'day to day pours forth speech' in Ps 19:3, as Metzudat Zion notes), so the wicked do not so much say things as overflow with them. The KJV's 'utter and speak hard things' loses the water and turns the pair of verbs into a single phrase; the Hebrew has two verbs for one act, and Radak says the doubling is for strength: they speak against You constantly. עָתָק, 'arrogance', is a hard, stiff, insolent word, the thing Hannah forbids in 1 Sam 2:3 (Metzudat Zion). The KJV's 'How long shall they...' borrows the question from v3, but the Hebrew has no 'how long' here: it is a flat statement. The last verb, יִתְאַמְּרוּ, is rare; Rashi and Ibn Ezra link it to Deut 26:17-18, where it means to declare or exalt, so these men 'lift themselves up' with their own talk. 'Workers of wickedness' (פֹּעֲלֵי אָוֶן) is a stock phrase in Psalms for the whole class of evildoers.

philological_notes.note: To bubble up, pour out like a spring; used of speech. The image is of uncontrolled outflow.
Hard, stiff, arrogant speech. The same word is used in 1 Sam 2:3.
Hithpael, 'to speak of oneself, to exalt oneself'. A rare form tied to Deut 26:17-18.

verses.translation_literal: Your people, YHWH, they crush, and your inheritance they afflict.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your people, LORD. Your own people, they grind them down, and your own inheritance, the land and the folk you took for yourself, they press until it cries out.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse turns from the boast of v4 to the victims, and the order of words does the accusing: "Your people" and "your inheritance" come first, each with the "your" attached, before the verbs. The speaker is not describing strangers. These are the ones YHWH claimed, and the wicked treat them as nobody's property. Say it close to the ear of God, as a complaint about ownership more than about pain. The two verbs sit in a pair. דכא is to crush, to pound to pieces (Metzudat Zion: כתיתה ושבירה, 'breaking and shattering'); ענה is to afflict, to humble by force (Metzudat Zion, from ענוי, 'affliction'). Both are in the piel, intensive, and both are imperfects: this goes on, day after day. Ancient courts were the one counterweight to this kind of pressure, and the Psalm's first lines have already called on the Judge of the earth to rise (v2). The KJV ("break in pieces") is close to the Hebrew; it only lengthens the verb into a phrase, and its "heritage" for נחלה is archaic where "inheritance" is the plain word, the family land that passes by lot and promise. Radak (on Ps 94:5) reads the verse with v6: the lawless wicked crush and afflict the Israelites who are strong and protected by the kingdom, as far as they are able, but the weak (the widow, the sojourner, the fatherless of the next verse) they kill, because those have no one to demand their blood.

philological_notes.note: To crush, to pound fine, said of the broken and the 'crushed in spirit'. The piel intensifies it, and the imperfect makes it a habit, not one blow.
'Your inheritance': Israel as YHWH's own share, as in Deut 32:9. The word is about land and family ties together, so crushing the people is a trespass on God's own estate.

verses.translation_literal: Widow and sojourner they kill, and fatherless ones they murder.
verses.translation_dramatic: The widow they kill. The stranger at the gate they kill. The child with no father they murder, and no one answers for it.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the list of the unprotected. Widow, sojourner and fatherless child are the three classes the Torah names again and again as God's own wards: they have no male head of house to avenge them, no land to anchor them. That is why they are the easy targets. Ibn Ezra reminds the audience of exactly this: the Torah says God 'does justice for the orphan and widow' (Deut 10:18), and the wicked, who kill those very people, are by that fact the enemies of the judge of the earth. The KJV's 'stranger' for גֵּר is a trap: the גֵּר is a resident alien, a person living long term under someone else's protection, with no kin of his own around him, as Radak says, so no one pursues his blood. The two verbs are not synonyms: הָרַג is to kill, and רָצַח (Piel here) is the word for illicit killing, murder. Ibn Ezra notes the Piel form is like 'this murderer'. Actors should not play this as a list but as a slow, flat count of the dead.

philological_notes.note: A resident alien, a person living under protection away from his kin. KJV 'stranger' makes him sound like a passing traveller.
Piel of the verb for unlawful killing, 'murder'. Radak asks whether it has a causative sense, 'they tell others to kill them'.

verses.translation_literal: And they said: Yah does not see, and the God of Jacob does not understand.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they say it, out loud, to each other: 'Yah does not see. The God of Jacob does not understand.'
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the root of it all: not rage but a theology. The wicked kill the powerless because they have decided that no one is watching. 'Yah', the short form of the divine name, is used here and in v12; it is archaic, poetic and slightly intimate, so its use by the wicked is irony: they speak of God lightly, with a nickname. The KJV's 'regard it' supplies an object ('it') that is not there. The verbs are simply 'see' and 'understand' (בִּין, 'discern'), the first for the eye and the second for the mind. Ibn Ezra explains the claim: they say God has no eye and no ear (and so, as the next lines will argue, the psalmist replies). Radak says it is the oppressors of Israel who say this, and that is why they do not fear Him. Note too 'the God of Jacob': they name Israel's own God by Israel's patriarch and so say that even a covenant God cannot be bothered.

philological_notes.note: The short form of the divine name YHWH, poetic and rare in prose. It reappears in v12.
To discern, understand, give thought. The pairing with 'see' is the usual pairing of eye and mind. Metzudat David: He does not set his heart to examine their deeds.

verses.translation_literal: Understand, stupid ones among the people, and fools, when will you have insight?
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen, you brutes among the people. Fools, when will you ever learn?
verses.directors_commentary: The voice turns on the listeners with a schoolmaster's snap. The verb 'understand' (בִּינוּ) is the same root as 'does not understand' in v7: the wicked said God cannot בִּין, and the psalmist throws the word back at them. Wordplay of that kind is the way Hebrew argues. The KJV's 'brutish' is accurate and rare in modern English; בֹּעֲרִים comes from בער, 'to burn' and 'to be brutish like cattle', so it means the dumb animal in a person. The BBE's 'give your mind to my words' reads something into the verb that is not quite there. Ibn Ezra thinks 'among the people' means that there are none as brutish as these in any people. Radak, more generally, reads it as 'among every people'. 'Fools' (כְּסִילִים) are the stubborn kind, who refuse to learn. The question 'when?' echoes the 'until when' of vv. 3: the wicked ask nothing, and now the psalmist asks them when they will stop.

philological_notes.note: The brutish, animal-stupid. Radak equates it with כסיל and בער; Ibn Ezra notes that it is formed on two patterns.
Hiphil: to act with insight, to grasp. Radak: 'how long will you stay in your folly?'

verses.translation_literal: The planter of the ear, does he not hear? Or the former of the eye, does he not look?
verses.translation_dramatic: The one who planted the ear: will he not hear? The one who shaped the eye: will he not see?
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the argument, in two questions, and the best-known one in the psalm. If God made the instrument, God has the capacity. The verbs are craftsman's verbs: 'plant' (נָטַע) is what a gardener does, so the ear is a thing set into the head like a seed, and 'form' (יָצַר) is what a potter does, so the eye is shaped. Ibn Ezra, noting the difference, says the ears are 'planted' because they sit fixed like two points of an axis, while the eye is 'formed' because images are formed in it all the time. The KJV is faithful here, and 'shall he not hear?' is exactly the sense of הֲלֹא; the BBE paraphrase loses the gardener and the potter. Note also 'look' (יַבִּיט) in the second half: it is not the plain verb of v7 'see' (רָאָה) but 'to look at, to gaze at attentively'. The wicked said 'he does not see', and the reply is 'he does not look closely?'. Rashi gives the point a human face: would the one who planted the ear not hear the cry of his people and their poor?

philological_notes.note: 'Is the planter of...?' The participle with the interrogative. A gardening image for the making of the ear.
Hiphil, to look at, gaze. A closer, more attentive verb than רָאָה ('see') in v7.

verses.translation_literal: The discipliner of nations, does he not rebuke? [He is] the teacher of humankind knowledge.
verses.translation_dramatic: The one who disciplines whole nations: will he not call you to account? The one who teaches humankind all it knows.
verses.directors_commentary: The argument widens from the single ear to whole peoples. 'Discipliner of nations' (יֹסֵר גּוֹיִם) points to history: Ibn Ezra and Radak list the flood, the scattering at Babel and Sodom, and Meiri adds Egypt, as events in which God was seen to correct a whole people. The KJV's 'heathen' is a loaded word for גּוֹיִם, which simply means 'nations'. The KJV's 'chastiseth' is fine; the Hebrew יָסַר is discipline as a parent does it, aimed at teaching, and the same verb returns in v12. The second half has no verb: literally 'the teacher of humankind knowledge'. The KJV supplies 'shall not he know?', which is the logic of v9 carried on; Ibn Ezra says the point is that human knowledge is nothing against the Most High, who is its source. In performance, let the second line drop away unfinished: the silence is the answer.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil, to reprove, set right, argue the case against someone. Rashi: 'he will discipline you for this.'
'Nations', peoples in general. KJV 'heathen' adds a religious contempt the word does not have here.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH knows the thoughts of humankind, that they are a breath.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD knows what a person thinks, and knows it for what it is: a breath, and gone.
verses.directors_commentary: A short verse after the questions, spoken as a verdict, almost quietly. 'Knows' is a participle (יֹדֵעַ), a continuous state: He is the one who goes on knowing. The key word is הֶבֶל, 'breath', which is the very name of Abel and the key word of Ecclesiastes: a puff of air, vapour on a cold morning. The KJV's 'vanity' is the Elizabethan way of saying emptiness, but it has come to mean pride in one's looks; in Hebrew the image is physical, something with no weight or lasting. 'They' (הֵמָּה) most naturally takes the thoughts as its subject, as Radak's second reading does: their plans amount to nothing and God can break them. Rashi aims it at those who think to exalt themselves with a crown and says they will learn it is a breath. Meiri notes the fine point: God knows these thoughts even though they are mere breath, so human lowliness does not hide a person from Him.

philological_notes.note: 'Breath, vapour', hence what is insubstantial and fleeting. Also the name Abel. KJV 'vanity' is the older English for the same idea of emptiness.
Thoughts, plans, designs. The word covers both inner reasoning and what a person intends to do.

verses.translation_literal: Happy the man whom you discipline, Yah, and from your Torah you teach him.
verses.translation_dramatic: How blessed is the one you take in hand, LORD, the one you teach out of your own law.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns from the accused to the believer, and from argument to consolation, using the beatitude form (אַשְׁרֵי) that opens the Psalter. The surprise is who is called blessed: not the man who is spared, but the man God disciplines. The same verb יָסַר from v10 returns, now for an individual, and with it the parental sense: Radak and Meiri quote Deut 8:5, 'as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you', and 8:16, 'to afflict you and test you, to do you good in the end'. The KJV's 'chastenest' is accurate but harsh to modern ears; the BBE's 'guided' softens it too far. 'Man' is גֶּבֶר, the strong man, a word that sets even the mighty under God's hand. 'Torah' means instruction before it means law: the KJV 'law' is narrower than the Hebrew, which is the teacher's word. Rashi (citing Tanchuma) says the righteous who are afflicted are happy provided that they occupy themselves with Torah and commandments. Notice that 'Yah' occurs in the middle of the line, a short, close name: the discipline is personal.

philological_notes.note: A plural construct, 'the happinesses of...' – the beatitude form. Not a wish but a declaration that this person's way is a good one.
Piel with a pronoun suffix, 'you discipline him'. The verb of a father correcting a child; see Deut 8:5.
'Your instruction', 'your teaching'. The sense of teaching comes before the sense of statute.

verses.translation_literal: To give quiet to him from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that he may be given quiet, a rest from the days of trouble, until the pit is dug for the wicked, and the ground is opened for them.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse finishes the sentence begun in v12: the man whom YAH disciplines and teaches is blessed so that he may be given quiet. The word is quiet (השקיט), not pleasure: calm after a storm, a land that "had rest" from war. Play it low and slow after the cries of the last verses. The wicked have noise, boasting and blood; the taught man waits, and his waiting has an end set by someone else. "Days of trouble" (ימי רע) are the stretch of bad times he must live through, in the plural: not one disaster, but a season. The second half is a hunter's image. A pit is dug for the beast, and an audience used to game traps and cisterns hears the patient work of digging, the point being that the digging is already in progress. The verb is כרה, to dig, in the passive (nifal): someone else is doing the work, and the wicked do not see it. The KJV is faithful here ("until the pit be digged") but its "adversity" for רע puts a moral word where Hebrew has the plain "bad, evil", and "give him rest" loses the stillness of השקיט. Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri read the "days of evil" as the days of judgment in Gehinnom, and the quiet as being spared them; Radak keeps to the plain sense that the righteous is untouched by the trouble while the wicked's pit is being dug.

philological_notes.note: Causative, 'to give quiet, to set at rest'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as הנחה, 'setting down', as one lays down a load.
'Is dug', the nifal of כרה, to dig. Metzudat Zion links it to 'he dug a pit' (Ps 7:16, cited by him as 'above', בור כרה).

'A pit' (Metzudat Zion: בור). The verb dug is כרה, a different word with a different root. Ibn Ezra takes the form to be from השחתה, 'destruction', and notes that the masculine verb יכרה agrees with a noun that is feminine in form only if שחת is read as a masculine noun like שוחד; so the pit and the ruin sound together here.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH will not abandon his people, and his inheritance he will not forsake.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD will not cast off his people. His own inheritance he will never leave behind.
verses.directors_commentary: The 'for' (ki) ties this to the cry of verse 5, where the wicked crush 'your people' and 'your inheritance'. Here the psalmist answers in the third person, as a teacher quoting a rule of the covenant: the same pair 'people' and 'inheritance' appear in Deuteronomy 32:9 and 1 Samuel 12:22. 'Inheritance' (nachalah) is land passed down in a family, a thing you do not sell. That is why the verb pairs matter: 'abandon' (natash) is to drop a thing in the field and walk away; 'forsake' (azav) is to leave a person alone. The KJV's 'cast off' is fine, but its 'neither will he' adds a negative link where the Hebrew has only 'and', and it makes a single thought out of the two clauses. The Hebrew word order puts 'his inheritance' first in the second line, a small stress. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as a reply to the earlier verses: they afflict your people, but he will not leave them for ever. Play it quietly and steadily, as a fact, not a hope.

philological_notes.note: To leave, abandon, let go; the idea of dropping a thing and walking off. It is paired with עזב (to forsake, leave someone) to make a full negation of desertion.
Inherited family land. Applied to Israel, it says that the people are God's own property and portion, not a thing he can swap.

verses.translation_literal: For to righteousness judgment will return, and after it, all the upright of heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: For justice will come home again to righteousness, and behind it will walk every upright heart.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the psalm, and the most compressed line in it. 'Judgment' (mishpat) is the act of a court: the verdict, the legal process. 'Righteousness' (tzedek) is the standard it should serve. The psalm says that these two have been pulled apart, by the judges who 'frame mischief by statute' (v. 20), and that the process will 'return' to its proper place. The verb 'return' (shuv) is the key: it says that justice has been away and will come back. Radak puts it in a picture of two companions separated, who find each other again. The KJV adds 'unto' and 'follow it' where the Hebrew has two bare phrases, 'to righteousness' and 'after it'; 'shall follow' is probably right, since the line is a procession, but a reader should know that the verb is the translator's. Malbim and Metzudat David read the line as a statement about delay and the suffering of the righteous; I follow the plainer sense. The 'upright of heart' are the ones whose inner life matches their outward conduct. A court is the place where outward and inward must agree.

philological_notes.note: Judgment: the verdict, the legal process and the right order that a court is meant to serve. The psalm opened with the 'judge of the earth' (v. 2), so the word returns the whole poem to its first image.
'Upright of heart': a standard phrase of the psalter for those whose character is straight, not bent. The heart is the seat of will and thought in Hebrew.

verses.translation_literal: Who will rise up for me with evildoers? Who will take his stand for me with workers of wickedness?
verses.translation_dramatic: Who will stand up for me when the evildoers rise? Who will plant his feet beside me, against the men who work wickedness?
verses.directors_commentary: The voice turns from 'his people' to 'I': the poet is in the courtroom himself. Two questions, in matching halves, with no answer given in the verse; the answer comes in the next one. The preposition 'im, 'with', is the trouble. It can mean 'beside' or 'against', and the translations split: the KJV chooses 'against' twice, YLT keeps the bare 'with', Radak says that it means 'against, as if fighting them'. The Hebrew word is the same in both halves, and I keep it. 'Rise up' and 'take one's stand' are the two postures of a witness or advocate in an ancient court, and also of a soldier. The 'workers of wickedness' (po'ale aven) is a stock name in the psalms for the wicked as a class, men whose trade is harm. Actors should hear the loneliness of the question: in a court of the elders at the city gate, the accused needs someone to stand up.

philological_notes.note: 'With': it can mean 'beside' (as an ally) or 'against' (as an opponent). The two English readings give opposite pictures: an advocate standing at my side, or a fighter facing them.
'Workers of wickedness': a regular phrase for the wicked as a class in the psalms. Aven means harm, trouble and the wickedness that causes it; the word comes back in v. 23 as 'onam.

verses.translation_literal: If not YHWH [had been] a help to me, like a little my soul would have dwelt in silence.
verses.translation_dramatic: Had the LORD not been my help, in a very little while my soul would have gone to live in silence.
verses.directors_commentary: The answer to the question of verse 16 is: nobody, except YHWH. 'Lulei' ('if not') begins a contrary-to-fact sentence, a thing that did not happen, so the tense is 'would have'. The Hebrew has no verb 'to be' and no 'would'; the English supplies both. 'Silence' (dumah) is the place of the dead. In Psalm 115:17 'the dead do not praise YHWH, nor any who go down into silence' (dumah), and the same word is used for the realm of the dead in Psalm 31:17. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all say that it is the grave. The KJV keeps 'silence', which is correct, but a modern reader will think of a quiet room; the Hebrew picture is of the land where nothing is said and nothing can be sung, which is worse for a psalm-singer than death itself. 'Soul' is nefesh: here it is the living person, the throat and breath, and Radak says exactly that. 'Like a little' (kim'at) means 'almost' or 'within a short time'. Say it low: a man who nearly stopped speaking for good.

philological_notes.note: Silence, and by extension the land of the dead (Ps 115:17, 31:18). Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as the plain word 'silence' (dumiyah); Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it as the place of the dead, the grave.
'My soul', but in Hebrew the living self, the breath and the life, not a separable spirit. Radak says it is the life-soul, the one that goes to the grave.

verses.translation_literal: If I said, "My foot has slipped," your steadfast love, YHWH, supported me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whenever I said, "My foot is slipping," your faithful love, O LORD, held me up.
verses.directors_commentary: 'If I said' is a habitual 'whenever': each time he felt the ground go, he was caught. The foot 'slips' (mot) as on a loose stone or a wet mountain path; the same verb is used for the earth shaking and for the righteous who 'shall never be moved' (Ps 15:5). 'I said' means 'I said in my heart', as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it, not out loud. The KJV 'mercy' for chesed is the usual weakness of English: chesed is covenant loyalty, the commitment a party keeps when it is not forced to, and 'mercy' makes it sound like a favour to a guilty man. The verb 'supported' (sa'ad) is of a staff or a hand under the arm; the KJV's 'held me up' is a good translation. The word order puts 'your chesed' first: 'it is your loyalty, O YHWH, that supports me'. The tenses are the hard point: 'said' is a perfect, 'supports' an imperfect; the KJV and ASV use the past for both, the BBE the present. The psalm lets both stand: it has happened, and it keeps happening.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: the commitment that holds even when the other party has no claim. 'Mercy' (KJV) is too narrow.
'It supports me': the root means a prop or staff, a hand under the arm. Metzudat Zion links it with 'support and propping'.

verses.translation_literal: In the multitude of my disquieting thoughts within me, your consolations delight my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: When the thoughts crowd in on me, thick and restless in my chest, your comforts come and make my soul glad.
verses.directors_commentary: Here is the interior of the man who was nearly silenced. 'Sar'afim' is a rare word: it occurs here and in Psalm 139:23 ('test me and know my thoughts'), and it names the thoughts that branch and run in many directions, the anxious thoughts of the sleepless. The KJV's plain 'thoughts' loses the restlessness. The contrast is carried by the word order: first 'in the multitude of my thoughts, within me', and only then 'your comforts'. 'Consolations' (tanchumim) is the plural of the word that, in the singular, names the comfort of Isaiah 40 ('comfort, comfort my people'), and Radak and Metzudat David read it as the promises of the prophets. The verb 'delight' (sha'ash'u) is a playful sound word, a Pilpel of a root meaning 'to dandle', as one plays with a child; Metzudat Zion cites Isaiah 11:8, the nursing child at the cobra's hole. The comfort of God does not argue the thoughts away: it plays with the soul as a mother does with a frightened child. Read the long first half fast and tangled, the second slow.

philological_notes.note: A rare word for the disquieting, branching thoughts of a troubled mind; elsewhere only Ps 139:23. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'thought'.
A Pilpel of the root meaning 'to dandle, play with, delight'. The doubling gives a sense of repeated, tender play; Metzudat Zion cites Isaiah 11:8 for the same verb of a nursing child.

verses.translation_literal: Will a throne of ruin be joined to you, one that fashions trouble by decree?
verses.translation_dramatic: Can a throne of ruin ever sit beside you, a throne that shapes misery into law?
verses.directors_commentary: A rhetorical question, and the answer is no. The psalm has called God the 'judge of the earth' (v. 2); now it asks whether the corrupt rulers on earthly thrones can claim a share in that office. 'Be joined' (chaver) is the verb for becoming a partner, an ally, a member of a company: could such a throne be your associate? 'Throne of havvot': havvah is ruin or disaster, the thing that falls apart; the KJV's 'iniquity' turns a word of consequence into a word of morals, though both senses are in play, since a throne of ruin ruins others. The line that follows is the real accusation: 'fashioning trouble by decree'. The verb 'fashion' (yatsar) is the potter's word; they mould harm out of the legal code itself, with a statute (choq) as the mould. The KJV's 'by a law' is acceptable, but 'frameth' is archaic and weak. This is not a gang breaking the law; it is a government writing the law to do the harm, which is why verse 21 follows with the court condemning innocent blood. Rashi and Radak read the throne as foreign: idol makers, or the throne of Nebuchadnezzar. The psalm itself names nobody.

philological_notes.note: Plural of havvah: ruin, destruction, calamity; a word for what falls apart. Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss it as 'breaking, shattering'. The KJV's 'iniquity' is a moral shift.
'Fashioning trouble by decree': yatsar is the potter's verb, choq a statute or engraved rule. The picture is of harm moulded into the shape of law.

token_glosses.gloss: will it be joined to you

verses.translation_literal: They band together against the life of the righteous, and innocent blood they declare guilty.
verses.translation_dramatic: They gather in a pack against the life of the righteous, and call innocent blood guilty.
verses.directors_commentary: Verse 20's decree is shown at work. 'Band together' (yagodu) is from gedud, a raiding troop, a gang with a captain; the verb implies a mob with a plan, not individual wrongdoers. Some medieval readers (Radak and Meiri mention them) take it as 'they cut' or 'decree', which fits the court setting, so the verb may carry both senses. The KJV's 'gather themselves together' is correct but flat. 'Against the life (nefesh) of the righteous' is a threat to the person himself, not to his goods. The second line is the heart of the matter, and the KJV obscures it: 'condemn the innocent blood' is a legal act. The verb is Hiphil of rasha, 'to declare guilty': they pronounce the verdict 'wicked' over blood that is naqi, clean. 'Innocent blood' is the phrase of Deuteronomy 19:10 and 21:8 for a killing that stains the land. So the court is the weapon, and the sentence is the murder. Rashi reads it just so: they 'hold him guilty in judgment to kill him'. The actors should not play a riot; they should play men in robes, entirely calm.

philological_notes.note: From the root of gedud, a marauding troop: 'they band together, form a troop'. Another reading ('they cut, decree') is mentioned by Radak and Meiri; I keep the troop sense.
Hiphil: 'to declare wicked, find guilty'. A legal verb, the opposite of declaring righteous (hitsdik). Rashi: 'they hold him liable in judgment, to kill him'.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH became for me a stronghold, and my God the rock of my shelter.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD became a high fortress for me, and my God the rock where I take shelter.
verses.directors_commentary: After the courtroom comes the cliff. 'Misgav' is a height too steep to be taken, a stronghold on a crag, and 'tsur' is the rock itself; 'machsi' is the shelter, the place you run to in a storm. The three words give a landscape of the Judean hills, where a fugitive hid in the rock and the cave. In this verse, as in the whole psalm, the man is no soldier: he flees to God as to a fortress. The KJV's 'defence' for misgav loses the image of height; its 'But' translates the connecting 'and' of the Hebrew, an acceptable contrast but not in the text. The verb 'became' (vayhi) is past: not 'is' but 'has turned out to be'. Meiri reads it as the end of the story told in advance. 'My God' (elohai) carries a personal claim that 'God' alone does not: this rock is mine. Say it plainly and let the rock be heavy.

philological_notes.note: A height too high to be reached: a stronghold on a crag. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'strength'. KJV 'defence' loses the image of height.
'Rock of my shelter': the rock is the place to which one runs, from the verb 'to take refuge'. A familiar double image in the psalms.

verses.translation_literal: And he brought back on them their wickedness, and in their evil he will destroy them; he will destroy them, YHWH our God.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has turned their own wickedness back upon them, and in their own evil he will cut them down. He will cut them down, the LORD our God.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends on its harshest note, and on a pun that the English hides. 'Their wickedness' is 'onam (from aven), and 'in their evil' is bera'atam (from ra'ah): the blow falls with the same weight as the crime. The verb 'brought back' (vayyashev) is the same shuv as in verse 15: justice 'returns', and so does their wickedness, onto their own heads. The punishment is the crime turned round. The KJV's 'their own iniquity' keeps this, but its 'yea' before the last clause is an addition: the Hebrew simply repeats 'he will destroy them' (yatsmitem, yatsmitem), a hammer stroke repeated, and it saves the divine name for the very end, 'YHWH our God', a deliberate delay. The verb tsamat means to silence, to put an end to; it recalls the 'silence' (dumah) of verse 17, the fate the psalmist escaped, now turned on the wicked. The KJV's 'cut them off' is accurate. The first verb is a wayyiqtol (past), the other two imperfects, and Radak reads the past as a certainty spoken of the future; I keep both. Read the last line slowly, with a drop on 'our God'.

philological_notes.note: 'Their wickedness / trouble', from aven, a word that returns from v. 16 ('workers of aven'). Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it instead to 'strength' (on); the sense 'trouble they made' suits the verse.
Hiphil: 'to put an end to, to silence, to cut off'. The verb is repeated in the verse, which Radak says is for emphasis. Metzudat Zion links it to Ps 101:5.
